segments.text: Contemporary movements challenge older assumptions about fixed foundations, detached reason, language, truth and human existence.

Existentialism emphasizes concrete existence, choice, anxiety, authenticity and responsibility, though Heidegger and Sartre differ. Pragmatism links meaning and inquiry with practical consequences and problem-solving. Rorty rejects strong foundationalism in favor of conversation/contingency. Postmodern thinkers question totalizing narratives, fixed structures of knowledge and stable meanings in different ways.

Existentialist thinkers differ substantially, but many focus on concrete human existence, freedom, anxiety, choice and the difficulty of living without ready-made guarantees. Heidegger analyses being-in-the-world and authenticity; Sartre emphasizes radical freedom, responsibility and the idea that human beings define themselves through projects and choices.
Existentialism does not simply mean pessimism. Its central concern is how persons confront finitude, contingency and responsibility.

Classical pragmatism connects meaning and inquiry with practical consequences and habits of action. Peirce emphasizes fallible communal inquiry; William James explores truth in relation to lived consequences and experience; Dewey treats inquiry as problem-solving within social life and education.

Richard Rorty’s neo-pragmatism rejects the ambition to represent reality from a neutral “view from nowhere” and stresses vocabulary, conversation and historically contingent practices. This is not the claim that every belief is equally good; justification still occurs within practices of reason-giving and criticism.

Foucault studies how institutions, practices and forms of knowledge help produce categories of normality, deviance and identity. His idea of power/knowledge stresses that systems of knowing human beings are intertwined with practices that classify, supervise and govern them.

Power in Foucault is not only something possessed by the state or a ruler. It operates through dispersed practices, institutions and norms, which is why his work is influential in studies of prisons, medicine, sexuality and administration.

Derrida’s deconstruction examines how texts depend on conceptual oppositions and exclusions that may be less stable than they appear. It is a disciplined form of reading that investigates how meaning is produced and deferred; it is not simply “destroying a text” or declaring that words can mean anything.
Critics argue that deconstruction can make normative judgment difficult or obscure; defenders see it as a way to expose hidden assumptions and marginalization within established concepts.

Lyotard is associated with skepticism toward large, universal “grand narratives” that claim to organize all knowledge and history. His analysis addresses the legitimation of knowledge in advanced societies rather than a simple denial of facts or truth.
A careful answer treats “postmodernism” as a family of debates rather than one doctrine shared identically by Lyotard, Foucault and Derrida.

items.text: Existentialism emphasizes concrete human existence, choice, anxiety, responsibility and authenticity, but Heidegger and Sartre do not present identical systems. Treat them separately.
Pragmatism connects meaning, truth and inquiry with practical consequences and problem-solving. Peirce, James and Dewey share a family resemblance but differ in emphasis.
Rorty's neo-pragmatism questions traditional foundationalism and the idea that knowledge mirrors reality from a neutral standpoint. He emphasizes contingency, language and conversation.

Postmodern thinkers should not be collapsed into one doctrine. Lyotard critiques grand narratives; Foucault analyzes relations among knowledge, power and institutions; Derrida develops deconstruction and examines instability and difference in textual meaning.
For each thinker prepare one central concept, a simple example, one criticism and one comparison. This turns abstract philosophy into exam-usable material.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not write “postmodernism says there is no truth” as a blanket statement. Explain the specific thinker's argument about knowledge, power, language or foundations.

items.text: Treat each thinker individually; do not merge them into one doctrine.
Prepare one core concept and one criticism for each.
Use plain-language examples to explain difficult terms.

segments.text: Pragmatism asks how ideas function in inquiry and experience.
Lyotard is associated with skepticism toward grand narratives.
Derrida is associated with deconstruction and instability in textual meaning.
